Title: FTIR study on the polymorphic structure of tricalcium silicate
Abstract: The infrared (IR) spectra of various tricalcium silicate (C3S) polymorphs were studied. The effects of variation in the polymorph and substituent ions on the IR spectra of C3S were discerned by synthesizing samples with differing types and amounts of foreign ions but the same polymorphic form. The IR spectrum of C3S mainly depends on the polymorphic form. Substituent ions have a weak influence. The IR spectra of T1 and T2 are very similar. Both show forbidden bands corresponding to symmetric vibration, indicating that [SiO4]4− tetrahedra are strongly distorted from an ideal tetrahedron. With an increase in the crystal symmetry of C3S, the number of bands for the polymorphs T1→T2→T3→M1→M3→R decrease, and the peaks become broader. The absence of symmetric stretching bands with a sharp peak at approximately 812cm−1 indicates that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra retain an approximately regular tetrahedron symmetry in T3, M1, M3 and R C3S.
1_Introduction:
Tricalcium silicate (Ca3SiO5, C3S) is the most important constituent of ordinary Portland cement clinker, exhibiting a complex polymorphism depending on the temperature and impurities [1–3]. Pure C3S can be triclinic (T1, T2, or T3), monoclinic (M1, M2, or M3), or rhombohedral (R) when heated. At room temperature, pure C3S only exists in the T1 form, and various impurities have to be introduced into C3S to obtain the other higher temperature forms [1–3]. Extensive efforts have been made to study the polymorphic structure of C3S in past decades. However, due to the complicated structure and the difficulty in preparing single crystals of C3S, the analysis of the crystal structure of C3S has been mainly based on powder X-ray diffraction (XRD), differential thermal analysis (DTA) and optical microscopy [1–3]. Consequently, the atomic structure of different C3S polymorphs and the relations between the polymorphs have not been fully understood. Only three polymorphs (R, M3, and T1) have been solved by X-ray single-crystal methods [4–9]. The measured structures are similar with respect to the positions of the Ca2+ and O2− ions and the Si atoms but differ markedly in the orientations of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, which show varying degrees of disorder [3,10]. The orientational disorder of the tetrahedra that characterize the M3 superstructure has features intermediate between those of R and T1 [8,10]. In addition, the mean coordination number of Ca2+ ions in M3 is also between those of R and T1 [8,10]. All C3S polymorphs, except T3 and R, have been confirmed to possess structural modulations [2,7,8,11–16]. The structural modulations of T1, M1, M2 and M3 C3S were systematically investigated by Urabe et al. using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) [11,12]. The superstructure of T1 was found to include both distortion of the silicate tetrahedra in their orientations and periodic deviation of cations from their average positions [11]. The monoclinic superstructures are believed to be caused by the periodic ordering of the orientations of the apices of the silicate tetrahedral [5,6,8,12]. With the development of Rietveld analysis and power diffraction, various structural models for T2, T3, M1 and M3 polymorphs have been developed based on the atomic models determined by the previous single-crystal experiments [14–20]. It has been shown that the structural differences between the polymorphs include slight shifts of the atomic positions and changes in the orientational order or disorder of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra associated with consequent changes in the coordination of calcium ions [2–20].
Infrared (IR) spectroscopy can be used to identify structures because molecules and functional groups absorb specific frequencies that are characteristic of their structure. The application of IR spectroscopy in the field of cement chemistry dates back to the 5th international symposium on the chemistry of cement, Tokyo (1968). As a simple, quick, and inexpensive analytical technique, IR spectroscopy can provide ample information on the structure of minerals and has been widely used to study cement and hydration products [21–33]. The IR spectra of pure C3S and its ion-stabilized forms have been studied [21–27]. However, changes in the IR spectra of C3S solid solutions were mainly attributed to the effect of substituent ions, and little attention has been given to the influence of variation in polymorphs.
Like C3S, dicalcium silicate (C2S) has a nesosilicate type structure with isolated [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, and the different C2S polymorphs mainly differ in the orientations of their [SiO4]4− tetrahedra. The vibration frequencies of C2S vary considerably depending on polymorphs [34]. Therefore, it is reasonable to hypothesize that variations in the polymorphs of C3S contribute to the differences in the IR spectra of C3S as well. Our recent research has shown that the IR spectra of C3S solid solutions (M3 form) with different compositions are similar but are quite different from that of T1 C3S [35]. However, there are few studies focused on the IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs due to the complexity of the C3S structure. The relations between foreign ions, the polymorphic structure and the IR spectra of C3S are not fully understood.
The main objective of this work is to obtain IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs and to understand the polymorphic structure of C3S. The effects of variation in the polymorphs and the introduction of substituent ions on the IR spectra of C3S were discerned by synthesizing samples with differing types and amounts of foreign ions but the same polymorphic form. The results from this study will help to further understand the polymorphic structure of C3S and to promote better use of IR spectroscopy in the study of cement and hydration products.
2_Material and methods:
2.1 Preparation of specimens C3S and its solid solutions were synthesized by a conventional ceramic method. Analytical grade chemical reagents CaCO3, SiO2, Na2CO3·10H2O, K2CO3, MgO, Al2O3, Fe2O3, BaO, CaHPO4·2H2O and CaSO4·2H2O were used as the starting materials. Table 1  shows the nominal dosages, expressed as oxide, used to prepare different polymorphs of C3S solid solutions. SiO2 was first calcined at 950°C to eliminate the volatile constituents and was then ground in an agate mortar for 1h to promote the formation of C3S. Second, a mixture of 3mol CaCO3 and 1mol SiO2 with different types and amounts of impurities was homogenized for 5h in a homemade mixer (prepared pure C3S was used as the starting material for single-ion doping). The mixtures were ground again in an agate mortar for 0.5h and then pressed into cylindrical pellets. The pellets were calcined at 1600°C for 6h and rapidly cooled with a flow of air. The samples were reground, pelletized and heated until a constant free lime (f-CaO) content was reached (less than 0.2%, mass weight, the same as below).
2.2 Testing method The free lime contents were determined by the ethylene glycol method. All powder diffraction data were recorded with a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffraction diffractometer in the range of 5–65° (2θ) with a step size of 0.01° using CuKα1,2 and a 1D position sensitive detector (PSD) (Lynxeye) at 38kV and 270mA. The Rietveld analyses of X-ray data were done using the Topas3 program. The Pearson VII function was used to fit the profile. The final globally optimized parameters were: zero shift, background, scaling factor, absorption correction, Pearson VII coefficients, lattice parameters and preferred orientation when appropriate. The atomic positions were not refined. FT-IR spectra of the samples were measured in the region 400–4000cm−1 using a Bruker TENSOR 27 Fourier transform infrared spectrometer. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns were recorded using a TEM instrument (Model JEM-2010UHR, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 200kV.
3_Results and discussion:
3.1 Analysis of C3S polymorphs All specimens were identified as C3S. The XRD peaks of C3S between 31.5° and 33° and between 51° and 52.5° are good indicators of the symmetries of the polymorphs [3,12,13]. Fig. 1  shows selected angular ranges of the XRD patterns (CuKα2 stripped) for the C3S samples. The differences between samples are evident. In the XRD pattern of R C3S, there are two characteristic peaks between 31.5° and 33°, and one between 51° and 52.5°, corresponding to the 009,   2 −  04  and 220 reflections, respectively. The   2 −  04  and 220 reflections split with a decrease in crystal symmetry of C3S. Pure C3S (Sample X1) is triclinic, T1, as expected, and both the   2 −  04  and 220 reflections are split into triplet peaks, presenting four reflections between 31.5° and 33° and three between 51° and 52.5°. The XRD pattern of T2 C3S is similar to that of T1 C3S. The main difference is that the central doublet peaks between 31.5° and 33° are closer for T2 C3S [12] and show a tendency to merge into a single peak. In the T3 powder pattern, there are only three peaks between 31.5° and 33°, and the last two peaks between 51° to 52.5° have a tendency to merge. In the monoclinic polymorph, the   2 −  04  and 220 reflections only split into doublets. Sample X4 presents phase coexistence. The main phase can be identified as M1 C3S [12]. Sample X5 presents an M3-type powder pattern [16]. Based on the X-ray diffraction data, quantitative analysis of C3S polymorph was performed using the Rietveld method. The T1 and T2 structures were fitted to that of Golovastikov et al. (triclinic C3S) [5]. T3 was fitted to the T3 structural model provided by De la Torre et al. [16]. M1 was fitted to the average monoclinic model provided by de Noirfontaine et al. [18]. The M3 and R structures were fitted to that of Nishi et al. (monoclinic) [8] and Jeffery (rhombohedral) [4], respectively. In Fig. 2 , the measured and calculated X-ray diffractions of different samples are shown together with the difference plots. The insets feature the fingerprint regions which are unique to different polymorphs. Table 2  gives the Rietveld quantitative phase analysis results of the C3S polymorph. It can be seen from Fig. 2 and Table 2 that the five samples (X1, X2, X3, X5 and X6) fit well with the corresponding structural model. However, two crystal structures are required to fit the XRD pattern of sample X4. Although the T1 structure of Golovastikov can be used for T3 C3S, the combined use of the T3 and M1 structure model resulted in better fits than the mixed use of T1 and M1, indicating that the quantification of C3S polymorphs is strongly affected by the choice of the structural model. TEM further confirmed that the main phase present in X4 is M1 C3S. Based on the pseudohexagonal subcell (a=7.062Å, b=7.063Å, c=25.026Å, α=89.89°, β=90.41°, γ=119.59°), a typical SAED pattern for M1 with a one-dimensional incommensurate structure was identified (shown in Fig. 3 ). It can be expressed as a linear combination of reciprocal vectors ±m/5.4 (2a H ∗ +5c H ∗), where m=±1 or ±2, in accordance with the data given by Urabe et al. [12] and Min et al. [36]. All polymorphs can be regarded as minute deformations of the rhombohedral structure [11–13]. The lattice parameters of the pseudohexagonal or hexagonal average structures (based on the R polymorph) for different polymorphs were refined by the least-squares method and are given in Table 3 . The lattice parameters of the M3 subcell are smaller than those of the other polymorphs, especially the parameter c and the cell volume. De la Torre et al. found that the unit cell volumes of M3 alite decrease with increasing amount of MgO by comparing the works of Mumme [9] and Nishi [8]. However, the MgO content of X5 is the same as sample X6, indicating that the shrinkage was probably related to the structure of the M3 polymorph rather than its composition. M3 C3S synthesized with different compositions also gave similar results. Viani et al. also found that there is a clear change in the lattice parameters and the thermal expansion coefficients of the monoclinic C3S solid solution (Ca2.879Mg0.112Al0.0439Si0.971O5) at approximately 900°C, which is due to the phase change between two monoclinic forms [37]. Thus, changes in the lattice parameters of M3 C3S are probably related to the variations in the polymorph. The differences in the deformation of the subcells of monoclinic C3S were attributed to differences in the ordering of the orientations of the apices of the silicate tetrahedra occurring along special directions (directions of the modulation waves) [12]. According to the literatures [4,7], silicon ions are on the c axis, approximately two of the three tetrahedra point down the c axis, and the others point up the cH axis in R C3S. However, there are additional ill-defined G–gauche–orientations in M3 C3S [8]. Thus, the shrinkage of the M3 subcell might correlate with unique changes in the arrangement of [SiO4]4− along the cH axis. More IR evidence will be discussed in the following sections.
3.2 IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs The infrared absorption bands of C3S in the region 400–4000cm−1 are mainly from the vibration of [SiO4]4− groups. Isolated [SiO4]4− tetrahedra have four vibration modes, including symmetric stretching vibration (ν1), asymmetric stretching (ν3), in-plane bending vibration (ν2) and out-of-plane bending (ν4). Ideally, the four Si-O sp3 hybrid orbits in a [SiO4]4− tetrahedron are completely equivalent with the same number of electrons on each track. These electrons repel each other and keep as far away as possible; thus, [SiO4]4− can maintain a regular tetrahedron symmetry when free of outside interference. Theoretically, the symmetric stretching ν1 of an ideal [SiO4]4− tetrahedron is not active for IR. The IR spectra of different C3S polymorphs are given in Fig. 4 , which shows that there is a decrease in the band splitting with increasing structural symmetry of C3S. The vibration bands for different C3S polymorphs are listed in Table 4 . The main vibrations of pure C3S (T1 form) are: symmetric stretching of the silicate tetrahedra [SiO4]4− (ν3) at 996, 938, 906 and 883cm−1; symmetric stretching (ν1) at 846, 834 and 812cm−1; out-of-plane bending vibration (ν4) at 525cm−1; and in-plane bending vibration (ν2) centred at approximately 464 and 455cm−1. These assignments are in accordance with the data given in previous studies [22–26]. The IR spectrum of T2 C3S is quite similar to that of T1 C3S. Both T1 and T2 C3S show forbidden bands corresponding to symmetric vibrations, indicating that the distortion from an ideal tetrahedron structure is caused by [SiO4]4−. This is supported by the finding of Peterson [14], who determined the structure of pure C3S with the T2 polymorph using in situ, high-temperature synchrotron powder diffraction combined with Rietveld refinement and showed that the SiO4 tetrahedra of T2 C3S were highly distorted and the OSiO bond angles showed significant deviation from the tetrahedral angle. Since the charge of the oxygen ion in [SiO4]4− was balanced by Ca2+ ions, the distortion of [SiO4]4− is probably due to the effect of the asymmetrical Ca2+ ion force field resulting from the poor structural symmetry of the T1 and T2 polymorphs. It is supported by the finding of Urabe et al., who found that cations periodically deviated from their average positions in T1 C3S [11]. Although T3 C3S belongs to the same triclinic system as T1 and T2, there are significant changes in the IR spectrum of T3. It has a smaller number of bands than the previous spectra. The symmetric stretching bands disappear, the most striking feature of which is that the sharp peak at approximately 812cm−1 vanishes, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra in T3 C3S retain a regular tetrahedron symmetry. This result is in agreement with the structural descriptions for T3 C3S given by De la Torre and Peterson [16,19]. Therefore, there are larger differences in the structure between T3 and T2 C3S than between T2 and T1 C3S. This conclusion is in agreement with the relatively large transformation enthalpy for the T2–T3 transition [2,13]. The T1–T2 transition has an extremely small transformation enthalpy and can be detected by microscopy, while the T2–T3 transition has a large transformation enthalpy and is invisible to light microscopy [38]. The collapse of the superstructure was first proposed by Bigare et al. [13] to explain the large peak in the DTA curve for the T2–T3 transition. This explanation was further supported by Peterson, who observed the existence of the superstructure in T1 and T2 for pure C3S using in situ, high-temperature synchrotron powder diffraction [14]. Regourd also suggested that the transition, which has no influence on the “megascopic” optical properties, might be attributed to the formation of the superstructure due to the orientation disorder of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra and changes in the Ca coordination [39]. Based on the above results from the IR spectra of T1, T2 and T3 C3S, this phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that the position of the Ca2+ and O2− ions and the Si atoms probably does not change, nor does the atomic packing density; consequently, there is no change in the refractive index. The large transformation enthalpy for the T2–T3 transition is mainly caused by changes in the deformation and orientation disorder of [SiO4]4− tetrahedra in the T2–T3 transition due to the displacement of the O atoms of [SiO4]4− tetrahedra, which also causes subsequent changes in the coordination of the surrounding Ca2+ ions. Despite the fact that there are major changes in the IR spectrum of T3 compared with that of T1 and T2, the IR spectra of the other three higher symmetry (temperature) polymorphs, M1, M3 and R C3S, are similar to that of T3, and only small shifts of the in-plane bending (ν2) to higher wave numbers were observed. The absence of the symmetric stretching bands shows that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra in M1, M3 and R have an approximately regular tetrahedron symmetry. Special shifts of the asymmetric stretching bands (ν3) at approximately 938cm−1 and 884cm−1 to 925cm−1 and 890cm−1, respectively, were observed for M3 C3S, which indicates that the chemical environment of [SiO4]4− in M3 C3S is different from that in the other polymorphs. It corresponds with the analytical results of XRD and can be explained by the changes in the arrangement of [SiO4]4− along the cH axis. With the increase in the crystal symmetry of C3S, the number of bands for the polymorphs T1→T2→T3→M1→M3→R decreases, and the peaks are broadened. The symmetric stretching bands with a sharp peak approximately 812cm−1 disappear in the spectra of T3, M1, M3 and R C3S, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra retain a regular tetrahedron symmetry in their structures. The structure of M3 C3S is slightly different from that of the other polymorphs with respect to the orientation of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra along the cH axis. The monoclinic superstructures are caused by periodical ordering of the orientations of the apices of the silicate tetrahedral [12]. Thus, the transitions between R, M3, M2 and M1 mainly involve changes in the orientation of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra. However, the differences in the superstructures of the average monoclinic and triclinic unit cells consist of both small displacements of calcium atoms and changes in the orientational order or disorder of the SiO4 tetrahedra [2]. The T3–T2 transition involves both local tetrahedral distortion of [SiO4]4− and changes in their orientation of. In T1 C3S, periodic deviations of cations from their average positions occurs, in addition to the distortion of silicate tetrahedral [11]. The relationship between C3S polymorphs remains unclear. To understand the atomic structure of the polymorphs and their relations, more work has to be done.
3.3 The effect of foreign ions on the IR spectra of C3S T1, T3 and M3 C3S with various types and amounts of foreign ions were systematically synthesized (see Table 5 ). Special attention is given to the amount of both Al2O3 and Fe2O3, which are amphoteric in nature and are usually considered top provide the best evidence to assess the effect of foreign ions on the IR spectra of C3S. Fig. 5  shows the IR spectra of T1, T3 and M3 C3S. The IR spectra of the C3S samples with different compositions but the same polymorphic form are almost identical. There are no changes in the peak position or number of peaks in the IR spectra of T1 C3S with single doping of either Al2O3 or Fe2O3 (see Fig. 5a). The IR spectra of T3 C3S with single doping of Al2O3 or Fe2O3 and with combined doping of multiple ions are shown in Fig. 5b. No changes are observed in the IR spectra of T3 C3S with different compositions. Similarly, no effect of Al3+ on the IR spectra of M3 C3S is observed (see Fig. 5c). However, Fe3+ has been shown to have a slight effect on the IR spectrum of M3 C3S. With increasing amount of Fe3+, slight shifts of the symmetric stretching bands (ν3) to lower waver number are observed for M3 C3S (Fig. 5c). However, the most intense peak is still centred at lower wave numbers of approximately 924–932cm−1, as described above. Thus, changes in the IR spectra of C3S solid solutions mainly result from changes in the polymorphic structures. The introduction of substituent ions has a weak effect on the IR spectra of C3S. Consequently, IR spectroscopy can be used to identify the polymorphs of C3S.
4_Conclusion: The following conclusions may be drawn from the present study.  1. The IR spectrum of C3S mainly depends on the polymorph or the mixture of polymorphs present. With increasing crystal symmetry of C3S, the number of absorption bands for the polymorphs T1→T2→T3→M1→M3→R decreases, and the peaks are broadened. The effect of substituent ions in C3S on the IR characteristics is weak. FTIR spectroscopy can be used to help identify the polymorphs of C3S.   2. The IR spectrum of T2 C3S is similar to that of T1 C3S. Both show forbidden bands corresponding to symmetric vibrations, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra are strongly distorted from an ideal tetrahedron.   3. Although T3 C3S belongs to the same triclinic system as T1 and T2, significant changes in the spectrum of T3 C3S are observed, indicating greater differences in the orientations and tetrahedral configurations of [SiO4]4− in T3 C3S than in T1 and T2 C3S. It explains why the T2–T3 transition has the largest transformation enthalpy but is invisible to microscopy methods.   4. The symmetric stretching bands with a sharp peak at approximately 812cm−1 are absent in the spectra of T3, M1, M3 and R C3S, indicating that the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra retain an approximately regular tetrahedron symmetry in their structures. The structure of M3 C3S is slightly different from that of the other polymorphs with respect to the orientation of the [SiO4]4− tetrahedra along the cH axis.
